mainTopic: Workers misled by a middleman hiring for the בעל הבית: why they have a complaint, and whose words they rely on when they say "as the בעל הבית said."
overview: The amud opens with the last lines of the משנה: whoever backs out of a work deal, or changes its terms, ends up at a disadvantage. The גמרא then explains the משנה's words "הטעו זה את זה" as a case where a middleman sent by the בעל הבית misled the workers he hired. If he offered less than allowed, the workers agreed, and if he promised more and said "your pay is on me," he owes it himself, as a ברייתא shows. So the case must be that he said the pay comes from the בעל הבית. The גמרא then explains the workers' complaint (תרעומת) in several ways: they lost a chance at a better job, or they were landowners who would not have worked for less, or they worked harder in a way that cannot be checked. Another answer says even a lower offer they agreed to gives them a complaint, because of the פסוק "אל תמנע טוב מבעליו." Next the גמרא asks a new question: if the workers said "as the בעל הבית said," do they rely on the middleman's report or on the בעל הבית's real offer? It tries to prove they rely on the middleman from a case of a גט sent through a שליח. רב אשי begins to respond, and his words continue on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing lines of the משנה: whoever backs out loses
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes: if the בעל הבית backs out, he is at a disadvantage. As a general rule, anyone who changes the deal or backs out is at a disadvantage.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the employer backs out, he loses out. Anyone who changes the terms loses out, and anyone who backs out loses out.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the final lines of the משנה. They give the general rule that whoever breaks or changes a work agreement is at a disadvantage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the משנה said that workers who back out lose out. Now it says the same about the בעל הבית. It then states a broad rule for both sides: the person who breaks the deal gets the worse end of any money dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: His hand is on the bottom, meaning he is at a disadvantage
The one who changes the agreed terms

steps.whatToRemember: Whoever changes the deal or backs out of it is the one who loses out.
steps.whyThisMatters: "כל המשנה ידו על התחתונה" is a well-known rule. It is used across the laws of hiring workers and craftsmen.

phrases.english: If the employer backs out,
his hand is on the bottom.
phrases.notes: An expression meaning he gets the worse deal when they settle up.

phrases.english: Whoever changes the terms is at a disadvantage,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַחוֹזֵר בּוֹ – יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה.
phrases.english: and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: An employer who backs out is at a disadvantage. In general, whoever changes or backs out of an agreement is at a disadvantage.

steps.title: Reading the משנה's wording: the workers misled each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the משנה said "they misled each other" and not "they backed out." So the case is one where the workers themselves misled one another.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה does not say "they backed out on each other." It says "they misled each other," which means the workers misled one another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the opening words of the משנה, "הטעו זה את זה." It draws a conclusion from the exact word the משנה chose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Had the משנה meant that the בעל הבית or the workers changed their minds, it would have said "חזרו." The word "הטעו" (misled) points to a different situation: one worker misled the other workers. That is why the only remedy is a complaint (תרעומת).

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
It does not teach, meaning the משנה did not use these words

steps.confusionAlert: The "each other" in the משנה does not mean the employer and the workers misled each other. The גמרא reads it as the workers misleading one another.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It does not teach "they backed out on each other,"
phrases.notes: The גמרא is going back to the opening line of this משנה: "השוכר את האומנין והטעו זה את זה."

phrases.english: rather "they misled each other,"
meaning that the workers misled one another.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״חָזְרוּ זֶה בָּזֶה״ לָא קָתָנֵי, אֶלָּא ״הִטְעוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's analysis of the משנה's opening phrase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "הטעו זה את זה" refers to the workers misleading one another, not to anyone backing out.

steps.title: How can workers mislead each other?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of case would have workers misleading each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the situation?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. It prepares for the גמרא to describe a real-life case that fits the words "they misled each other."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the בעל הבית hires the workers directly, so it is hard to see how one worker could mislead another. The גמרא needs a case where one worker is in charge of the hiring.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does this situation look?

phrases.english: What is the case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a concrete case that fits the reading in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A realistic case in which workers mislead other workers.

steps.title: The case: a worker sent to hire others
steps.stepSummary: The בעל הבית told one worker to go hire workers for him, and that worker misled the workers he hired.
steps.simpleTranslation: The employer told him, "Go hire workers for me," and he went and misled them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The case involves a middleman, one worker whom the בעל הבית sent to do the hiring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains how workers can mislead workers: one of them acts as the hiring agent and tells the others something untrue. The next question is what exactly he told them.

phrases.english: Where the employer said to him:
"Go, hire workers for me,"
and he went and misled them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת: זִיל, אֲוגַר לִי פּוֹעֲלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A middleman sent by the employer to hire workers misled the workers he hired.

steps.title: If he offered less than allowed, there is no complaint
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the misleading was. If the בעל הבית allowed four and the middleman offered three, the workers have nothing to complain about, because they knowingly agreed to three.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the employer told him four, and he told them three, what room is there for a complaint? They knew and agreed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first way the middleman might have misled the workers. It rejects it, because the workers agreed to the lower wage with full knowledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the workers have only a תרעומת (a complaint). In this option they don't even have that. Their own deal was three, and they accepted it. So this cannot be the משנה's case.

keyTerms.meaning: A complaint or grievance, a moral claim with no money owed
What is it doing here? What place does it have?

phrases.english: What is the case?

phrases.aramaic: אִי דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בְּאַרְבְּעָה,
phrases.english: If the employer told him four,
phrases.notes: Four coins per day of work. Below, "three" means three coins.

phrases.english: and he went and told them three,
what place is there for a complaint?
They understood and accepted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Probes the case given in step 4 by testing the first possible way the middleman misled the workers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the misleading was offering the workers less than the employer authorized.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The workers knowingly agreed to the lower wage, so they would not have even a complaint. Yet the משנה says they do have one.

steps.title: If he offered more than allowed, he may owe it himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the opposite case: the בעל הבית allowed three and the middleman promised four. If the middleman said "your pay is on me," he should pay the extra from his own pocket, which is more than just a complaint.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the employer told him three, and he told them four, what is the case? If he told them, "Your pay is on me," let him pay them from his own money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second option. It shows that in one version of it, the middleman would truly owe money, which does not fit the משנה's "only a complaint."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the workers really were misled into expecting more pay. But if the middleman took the pay on himself, he is legally responsible for the full four, so the workers have a real money claim. The גמרא still needs a version of this case that leaves only a complaint, and it keeps searching after this.

keyTerms.meaning: Your wages are on me, meaning I take responsibility for your pay

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא has not finished defining the case yet. This step only shows that "your pay is on me" cannot be the משנה's case. The search continues afterward.

phrases.aramaic: אִי דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בִּתְלָתָא,
phrases.english: If the employer told him three,
and he went and told them four,
what is the case?
If he told them, "Your wages are on me,"
let him give it to them from his own money,
phrases.notes: He pays the extra amount the employer did not agree to.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ: ״שְׂכַרְכֶם עָלַי״ – נִתֵּיב לְהוּ מִדִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first option fails in step 5, tests the opposite option.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the misleading was the middleman promising more, while saying "your pay is on me."
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A middleman who takes the pay on himself owes the full promised wage. That is a real money claim, not just a complaint.

steps.title: ברייתא: whoever hires is responsible for the full wage
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the claim that the hirer pays. Someone hired a worker for his own field but by mistake showed him another person's field. He must pay the worker in full, and then collect from the field's owner only the value of the benefit that owner got.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: one who hires a worker to work in his own field, and shows him another person's field, gives him his full wages. Then he goes back and takes from the field's owner the value of the benefit he gave him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove the previous step: whoever hired the worker is responsible for paying him in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the hirer pays the full wage even though the work went to someone else's field. He can only collect back the benefit the other owner received. In the same way, a middleman who said "your pay is on me" must pay the full promised amount himself, and the בעל הבית pays only what he agreed to.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
The value of the benefit he gave him

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא sets the rule that the person who makes the hiring promise is personally responsible for the wage. Anyone who gained from the work owes only the value of what he gained.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַפּוֹעֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּשֶׁלּוֹ
phrases.english: As it was taught: One who hires a worker to work in his own field,
and showed him a field belonging to his fellow,
gives him his wages in full,

phrases.aramaic: וְחוֹזֵר וְנוֹטֵל מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת מַה שֶּׁהֶהֱנָהוּ.
phrases.english: and goes back and takes from the owner the value of the benefit he gave him.
phrases.notes: Here בעל הבית means the owner of the other field, the one who got the free work.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַפּוֹעֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּשֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim in step 6 that the middleman must pay from his own pocket.
steps.raayaObject: A person who takes responsibility for the hiring pays the full wage himself.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a hirer who mistakenly sent his worker to another person's field. He pays the full wage and collects only the benefit from the other owner.

steps.title: The middleman said the pay comes from the employer
steps.stepSummary: The middleman owes no money himself, because he told the workers their wages would come from the בעל הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is needed where the middleman told them: Your pay is the responsibility of the בעל הבית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6: why does the middleman not have to pay the extra amount himself? Because he never took the pay on himself. He told the workers the בעל הבית would pay them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 7 showed that a hirer pays when the debt is his own. Here the middleman said 'your pay is on the בעל הבית,' so the debt was never his. The workers are left with only a complaint (תרעומת) against him, not a claim for money.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not needed [except for]' — the case we need is this specific one
The employer who owns the field

phrases.english: No, it is needed

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ שְׂכַרְכֶם עַל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: where he said to them: Your wages are on the employer.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the middleman, who promised four when the בעל הבית had only agreed to three.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ שְׂכַרְכֶם עַל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6, which was backed by the ברייתא in step 7, by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The middleman promised the money himself, so he should pay the difference.
steps.terutzMaskana: He put the pay on the בעל הבית, so he owes nothing, and the workers have only a complaint.

steps.title: Just pay them the usual local wage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the workers should feel cheated. Pay them whatever workers usually earn in that place.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us see how much workers are usually hired for, and pay them that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the case: if there is a normal rate for workers in that place, use it, and there is no real loss to complain about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the usual wage is four, the בעל הבית should pay four. If the usual wage is three, the workers were never going to get more anyway. Either way, it seems there is nothing for the workers to complain about.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us see / let us check

phrases.english: But let us see how much workers are hired for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the idea that the workers have any real complaint in the case of step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the workers have a complaint against the middleman
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A local standard wage settles the pay, so the workers lose nothing.

steps.title: Wages in that place are mixed, so they could have found four
steps.stepSummary: In that place some workers get four and some get three. The workers say: had you not promised four, we would have searched and found a job at four.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where some workers are hired for four and some for three. They tell him: If you hadn't told us four, we would have made the effort and found a job at four.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is no single local rate. Because of the middleman's promise, the workers stopped looking for a better-paying job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since there is no fixed rate, the בעל הבית may pay the lower amount of three. The workers lost a real chance at four because they trusted the middleman, and that loss is their complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: If not / had it not been
We would have made the effort

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there are some who are hired for four
and there are some who are hired for three,
so they say to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the middleman who hired them.

phrases.english: Had you not told us four,
we would have made the effort and been hired for four.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִיכָּא דְּמִתְּגַר בְּאַרְבְּעָה וְאִיכָּא דְּמִתְּגַר בִּתְלָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by setting the case in a place without one fixed wage.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There is a standard wage that settles everything.
steps.terutzMaskana: Wages vary, and the workers lost the chance to find work at four.

steps.title: Second answer: the workers were landowners
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: the workers own their own land. They say: we would never have taken a job for less than four, because it is beneath us.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: here we are dealing with landowners. They tell him: If you hadn't told us four, it would have been beneath us to hire ourselves out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer that works even where there is a fixed local wage. These workers would only take the job because of the higher promise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A landowner who works for others only does it if the pay is worth it. Because of the middleman's promise, they took a job they would have turned down at the lower pay, and that is their complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say — introduces another answer

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'בעל הבית' does not mean the employer. It means the workers themselves, who own land and are not regular laborers.

phrases.english: If you want, say:
Here we are dealing with a landowner,
so they say to him:
Had you not told us four,
it would have been beneath us to hire ourselves out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָכָא בְּבַעַל הַבַּיִת עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 9, given alongside the answer in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative narrowing of who the workers are
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A fixed local wage leaves no grounds for complaint.
steps.terutzMaskana: These workers took the job only because of the higher promise, so they have a complaint.

steps.title: Third answer: they worked extra hard
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: they are regular workers. They say: because you promised four, we worked extra hard and did fine work for you.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: really we are dealing with regular workers. They tell him: Since you told us four, we made the effort and did excellent work for you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer: regular workers whose complaint is that they put in better effort because of the promised pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the loss is not a missed job but extra effort. They gave four-dinar quality work and are getting three. This sets up the next challenge: can't the work be checked?

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually — keeping the first way of reading the case

phrases.english: If you want, say:
really we are dealing with workers,
and they say to him:
Since you told us four,
we made the effort and did fine work for you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to step 9, going back to regular workers.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative explanation of the workers' loss
steps.terutzMaskana: They gave extra effort because of the promise.

steps.title: Just look at their work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: let us check their work. If it really is better, pay them more.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us look at their work!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the third answer. If the work is visibly better, it can be judged, and they should be paid for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If extra-good work can be seen, the בעל הבית would pay for it and the workers would lose nothing. That would undo the complaint from step 12.

phrases.english: But let us see their work?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the third answer from step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that their extra effort is a loss
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Better work can be seen and paid for, so they lose nothing.

steps.title: The work was digging the soil
steps.stepSummary: The work was digging up the ground, where you cannot easily see how good the job was.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was digging the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the job was the kind of work whose quality is hard to see.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With digging, the result does not clearly show how deep or careful the work was. So the extra effort cannot be checked and paid for.

phrases.english: It was digging the soil.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by naming the kind of work.
steps.terutzMaskana: Digging is work whose quality is hard to see.

steps.title: Can't you check digging too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even with digging, can't you tell how well it was done?
steps.simpleTranslation: With digging too, isn't it known?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer: you could look at the dug ground and see how deep it goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dug earth can be inspected, so the quality should still be visible. That would bring back the challenge of step 13.

phrases.english: With digging too, it can surely be known?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that digging cannot be checked
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dug ground can be inspected, so the effort is visible.

steps.title: The dug area filled with water
steps.stepSummary: The dug area filled up with water, so no one can see how well the work was done.
steps.simpleTranslation: It filled with water, so it cannot be known.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final answer: water covered the digging, so its quality really cannot be checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the work is now hidden under water, the בעל הבית cannot see the extra effort or pay for it. So the workers' complaint from step 12 stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The middleman owes nothing because he put the pay on the בעל הבית. The workers still have a fair complaint: they missed a job at four, or they took a job they would have turned down, or they worked extra hard in a way no one can check.

phrases.english: Where it filled with water, and it is not known.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15 and so protects the third answer from step 12.
steps.terutzMaskana: Water hides the work, so the extra effort cannot be seen and the complaint stands.

steps.title: Another answer: the employer offered four and the middleman said three
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the simple case: the בעל הבית offered four, but the middleman told the workers three. The workers can still complain, because he held back money that was meant for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say this instead: really, the employer told the middleman to hire for four, and the middleman went and told the workers three. And as for what you asked, 'They knew and agreed, so why complain?', the workers can say to him: 'Don't you know the פסוק "Do not withhold good from the one it belongs to"?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a fourth answer. It goes back to the simplest version of the case and explains why the workers still have a grievance even though they agreed to three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא asked: if the workers agreed to three, why should they complain at all? This answer says agreeing does not end the matter. The middleman held back extra money that was meant for them, so they have a fair תרעומת against him, though no claim to collect money.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (another answer is coming)
Really, actually (we stay with the original case)
Do not withhold good from the one it belongs to (משלי 3:27)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a person can have a fair grievance, a תרעומת, even when there is no claim to collect money in court.

phrases.english: If you wish, say: actually
the employer told him to hire for four,
and he went and told them three,
and as for what you said, 'they knew and accepted',
they can say to him: Don't you have
'Do not withhold good from the one it belongs to'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first option rejected in step 5 (employer said four, middleman said three) and answers that step's challenge 'סבור וקביל' with a פסוק. This is an alternative to the whole line of answers in steps 6–16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Returns to the simple case and answers the challenge 'they agreed' with a פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the workers knowingly agreed to three, we might think they have no grievance at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: They have a fair תרעומת, because the middleman held back good that was meant for them.

steps.title: The obvious case: the employer said three, the middleman said four
steps.stepSummary: If the בעל הבית said three, the middleman said four, and the workers said 'as the בעל הבית says,' they clearly meant the higher amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if the employer said three, and the middleman went and told the workers four, and they answered, 'We'll take whatever the employer said,' they meant the extra, higher amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by stating a case whose answer is clear. This sets up the harder question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the workers said 'as the בעל הבית says,' they were only hoping he might offer even more. They never meant to accept less than the four they were already told.

keyTerms.meaning: Their intent was for the higher amount

phrases.aramaic: פְּשִׁיטָא אִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בִּתְלָתָא,
phrases.english: It is obvious: if the employer told him three,
and he went and told them four,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לֵיהּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת –
phrases.english: and they told him, 'as the employer said',
their intent is for the additional amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא אִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בִּתְלָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה's case to a new related question about what the workers' words mean.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the workers say 'as the בעל הבית says,' they intend the higher amount and not less than what they were told.

steps.title: The harder case: whose words are the workers relying on?
steps.stepSummary: If the בעל הבית said four, the middleman said three, and the workers said 'as the בעל הבית said,' did they trust the middleman's report or the בעל הבית's real offer?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the employer said four, and the middleman told them three, and they said, 'We'll take what the employer said,' what is the law? Are they relying on the middleman's words, as if saying, 'We trust you that this is what the employer said'? Or maybe they are relying on what the employer actually said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a real question it does not yet know the answer to. In this case, which amount do the workers get?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the workers trusted the middleman's report, they agreed to three. If they meant whatever the בעל הבית truly offered, they are owed four. The question is what their words 'as the בעל הבית said' really meant.

keyTerms.meaning: They rely on his (the middleman's) words

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the previous step. There the middleman said MORE than the בעל הבית, and the answer was obvious. Here he said LESS, and that is why there is a question.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בְּאַרְבְּעָה,
phrases.english: But if the employer told him four,
and he went and told them three,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי: כְּמָה שֶׁאָמַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת, מַאי?
phrases.english: and they said, 'as the employer said', what is the law?
Do they rely on his statement,
phrases.notes: 'His' means the middleman, the one who actually spoke to them.

phrases.english: as they say to him: We trust you
that this is what the employer said,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אַדִּיבּוּרָא דְּבַעַל הַבַּיִת קָא סָמְכִי?
phrases.english: or perhaps they rely on the employer's statement?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בְּאַרְבְּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After stating the obvious case, the גמרא asks about the opposite case, which is not obvious.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether workers who say 'as the בעל הבית said' rely on the middleman's report (three) or on the בעל הבית's actual offer (four).

steps.title: Opening a proof from a woman who sends for her גט
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to bring a proof from the laws of גט, starting with a woman who tells a שליח, 'Bring me my גט.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a woman said, 'Bring me my גט.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a proof to answer the question. It starts quoting a case about a woman who sends a messenger to bring her גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of the גט deals with a similar problem: who do people rely on when a messenger reports someone else's words? The rest of the case, which comes next, will be used to answer the question about the workers.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a proof is coming)
Bring me my bill of divorce

phrases.english: Come and hear: 'Bring me my bill of divorce.'
phrases.notes: A woman is saying this to a messenger. The rest of the case continues right after this line.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins an attempt to answer the question in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether the workers rely on the middleman's words or on the בעל הבית's words.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case about a woman who tells a שליח, 'Bring me my גט' (it continues after this line).

steps.title: The שליח changes her words, and רב rules she is not divorced
steps.stepSummary: The שליח tells the husband the woman said 'receive my גט,' the husband says 'take it as she said,' and רב rules she is not divorced even once the גט reaches her.
steps.simpleTranslation: The שליח told the husband: 'Your wife said, Receive my גט for me.' The husband said: 'Here it is, as she said.' רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה in the name of רב: even if the גט reaches her hand, she is not divorced.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes describing the גט case it started in step 20 and gives רב's ruling. She is not divorced at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The woman only asked for a delivery agent ('bring me'), but the שליח told the husband she wanted a receiving agent ('receive for me'). A receiving agent would make her divorced the moment he gets the גט. רב says that here she is not divorced even when the גט finally reaches her hand, which tells us something about how the husband understood the agent.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Receive my גט for me': this makes the שליח a receiving agent, so she is divorced as soon as he gets it
An agent the woman appoints to receive the גט for her
An agent who only carries the גט to her; she is divorced when it reaches her hand

steps.confusionAlert: The woman herself said 'bring me my גט' (step 20). The words 'receive my גט' are the שליח's changed version, not what she really said.

phrases.english: And [the שליח told the husband:] Your wife said, 'Receive my גט for me,'
phrases.notes: This is the שליח talking. She really said 'bring me my גט,' and he changed it.

phrases.english: and he [the husband] says: 'Here it is for you, as she said.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Rabba bar Avuh said that Rav said:
Even if the גט reaches her hand,
she is not divorced.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ אָמַר רַב: אֲפִילּוּ הִגִּיעַ גֵּט לְיָדָהּ – אֵינָהּ מְגוֹרֶשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the גט case begun in step 20 and gives its ruling
steps.raayaObject: The question from step 19: did the workers rely on the middleman's report or on the בעל הבית's real offer?
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's ruling that the woman is not divorced even when the גט reaches her hand

steps.title: The husband relied on the שליח's words
steps.stepSummary: From רב's ruling, the גמרא learns that the husband relied on what the שליח said, not on what the woman really said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this that he relies on the שליח's words. For if you thought he relies on her words, then at least once the גט reaches her hand she should be divorced.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from רב's ruling: the husband went by the שליח's report. If this holds, it would answer the workers' question in favor of the middleman's report. The next step shows רב אשי responding to this proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the husband had gone by the woman's real words ('bring'), the שליח would be a delivery agent, and she would be divorced once the גט reached her hand. Since רב says she is not divorced even then, the husband must have gone by the שליח's version ('receive'). That version was false, since she never made him her receiving agent, so nothing works. In the same way, the workers relied on the middleman's report of three.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Learn from this': the גמרא is drawing a conclusion
'If it would enter your mind': introduces an idea the גמרא is about to reject

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the proposed proof for step 19: people rely on what the go-between tells them. If it holds, the workers who said 'as the בעל הבית said' accepted three, the middleman's number. רב אשי's response in the next step tests this proof.

phrases.english: Learn from this
that he relies on his words.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the husband, and 'his words' are the שליח's report.

phrases.english: For if it would enter your mind
that he relies on her words,
then once the גט reaches her hand,
at least then she should be divorced.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁמְעַתְּ מִינַּהּ אַדִּיבּוּרָא דִּידֵיהּ קָא סָמֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from רב's ruling in step 21
steps.raayaObject: Whether a person relies on the go-between's report or on the original speaker's real words
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fact that she is not divorced even when the גט reaches her hand shows the husband relied on the שליח's words

steps.title: רב אשי begins to respond
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי begins a response to the proof from the גט case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. רב אשי is about to answer the proof, and his words come in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An answer from another אמורא right after a proof usually means the proof is about to be challenged. Wait for רב אשי's words to see how he deals with the גט case.

keyTerms.meaning: A late אמורא who often gives the final answer in a סוגיא

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a response to the proof in step 22
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the גט case (content continues in the next part of the גמרא)
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Not yet stated. רב אשי's reasoning follows.
